title: Padroni Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Padroni well data: median depth 180 feet, median yield 15 gpm, and estimated finished-well costs of $12,300-$21,900.
h1: What Padroni, Colorado Wells Are Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Padroni means looking closely at the local well record, not relying on a countywide average. Within 5 miles of Padroni, Colorado, DWR records include 422 permitted wells, with 278 recorded as constructed. The available records point to generally productive wells, but depth and water levels vary across the plains.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and many also list stock water. Before you buy or build, compare nearby well permits, confirm the intended use with Colorado DWR, and have a driller evaluate the exact parcel. A good production result nearby is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee for a new hole.

sections.heading: Padroni Well Depths Depend on the Local Sediments
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Padroni is 180 feet. The middle half runs from 54 to 310 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should not treat 180 feet as a guaranteed target. The broad spread reflects changing plains sediments and sedimentary rock across the area.

Forty-one percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 28% fall from 100 to 300 feet and 31% from 300 to 600 feet. The deepest record is 600 feet. For a buyer, that distribution means a shallow nearby well does not eliminate the possibility of a deeper bid on your lot. Ask for a written estimate that explains the assumed depth, casing and grout, and what happens if drilling must continue.

sections.heading: Most Padroni Wells Report Strong Production
sections.html:
Only 86 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield data is a sample rather than a result for every permitted well. Among those records, the median yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Twenty-nine percent fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 1% are in the 1-to-5 range and 0% are under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for household use, but a pump-yield figure is not the same as guaranteed long-term supply. Have the driller explain the test method, recovery, storage tank needs, and the permitted use before you size a home system.

sections.heading: Padroni Water Levels Show a Wide Range
sections.html:
Static water-level data is limited to 20 wells. The median depth to water is 37 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 104 feet. That range matters during construction because a shallow water level can affect drilling conditions, casing, trenching, and the final pump setup.

The available facts do not provide water-level measurements by decade, so they do not establish a dropping or rising regional water table. Do not read the 37-foot median as a parcel-specific guarantee. Request the original well construction and test records for nearby properties, then ask a licensed driller how seasonal conditions and the local aquifer affect the proposed location.

sections.heading: Padroni Permit History Identifies Local Drillers
sections.html:
Permit activity near Padroni extends from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2026. The records show 17 permits in the 1950s, 46 in the 1960s, 42 in the 1970s, 40 in the 1980s, 41 in the 1990s, 61 in the 2000s, 52 in the 2010s, and 12 in the 2020s.

The most common drillers in these records are Stewart Drilling Co. (Stewart, Dennis W.) with 55 wells, M&S Drilling, Inc. (Monheiser, Mark) with 38, and Canfield, Leslie George with 29. These names show local permit history, not an endorsement. Confirm current licensing, availability, insurance, scope of work, and references before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: A Padroni Well Costs More Than the Drilled Hole
sections.html:
For Padroni's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 180-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $6,300 to $9,900. That figure is not the complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,300 to $21,900 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median hole can increase the total, and the site layout can change trenching and electrical costs. When comparing bids, ask whether casing, grout, development, pump testing, permits, wiring, and connection to the house are included or priced separately.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Yield, Septic Space, and Building Plans
sections.html:
Environmental review within about 10 miles identifies 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features mapped in that area. Those records do not prove contamination on a particular lot, but they are a reason to obtain a current laboratory water test and review nearby site information before closing.

Most permitted wells name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 404 wells in that category; 6 name the Ogallala and 5 name Quaternary Alluvium. Fractured formations can be unpredictable even when nearby wells perform well. Also confirm septic setbacks, drainfield space, driveway access, building location, and the well's permitted use. Household wells are not automatically authorized for every future use, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Use Nearby Records Before Buying or Building
sections.html:
Start with wells on adjoining parcels, then expand the comparison toward Iliff, Sterling, Peetz, Atwood, Fleming, and Crook. Look for construction depth, aquifer name, yield test, static water level, permit status, and permitted use. The Padroni records list domestic or household use on 68% of permits, stock use on 44%, irrigation on 7%, and monitoring on 3%, so do not assume a stock or irrigation permit can serve a residence.

For a purchase, make water rights, well records, inspection, and water-quality testing part of due diligence. For a build, locate the well, septic system, driveway, and utility routes together before excavation. A driller can refine the depth and pump budget after reviewing the parcel and neighboring records, but no map can promise that a new well will match the local median.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Padroni, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Padroni is 180 feet. The middle half ranges from 54 to 310 feet. Forty-one percent are under 100 feet, 28% are between 100 and 300 feet, and 31% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 600 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Padroni?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 180-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,300 to $9,900. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,300 to $21,900. A deeper hole or difficult site can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water can a Padroni well produce?
faq.a: Yield data is available for 86 wells. The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures describe recorded tests, not a guarantee for a new well on a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Padroni?
faq.a: The available well records do not establish that every Padroni well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, there are 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the existing well tested by a certified laboratory, and test a new well before use. Review local environmental information as part of due diligence.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Padroni?
faq.a: Check the Colorado DWR permit, construction depth, permitted use, yield test, static water level, casing and grout records, and recent laboratory results. Nearby records include 422 permitted wells, but only 278 are recorded as constructed and 20 report static water levels. Confirm that the well supports the planned home, septic layout, livestock, and any other intended use.
